learning_outcomes.text: Be familiar with the concept of function/sequence and their limits; use these to understand the notion of derivative and, consequently, be able to locally approximate functions using polynomials. Have a solid understanding of Riemann integration theory, including possible generalizations, and be able to apply it to the computation of integrals. Know various convergence criteria for numerical series and understand their relation to improper integrals.

Be able to construct and develop logical arguments with a clear identification of assumptions and conclusions. Apply the theoretical knowledge acquired to the solution of concrete problems, including those of intermediate complexity, through extensive classroom practice. Understand its applicability in applied courses.
Evaluate the coherence and correctness of obtained results; analyze appropriate solution strategies for the proposed exercises, based on their own knowledge.

Use formally correct language to communicate the course content in a clear, precise, and concise manner. Lectures and direct interaction with the instructor will support the acquisition of a specific and appropriate scientific vocabulary, enabling the student to communicate clearly and accurately even beyond purely computational contexts.

Independently deepen their knowledge, starting from the foundational material provided in the course, in order to effectively manage the use of additional tools and concepts from mathematical analysis, both in subsequent courses and in individual study.

Begin to develop a flexible mindset that enables them to adapt easily to new problems, work both independently and in groups, acquire new knowledge through self-study, and efficiently retrieve information from available literature and sources.

syllabus_topics: Numerical sets: natural numbers and induction principle
Complex numbers and their n-th roots

Real functions: maximum and supremum; monotone, odd and even functions; powers; irrational functions; absolute value; trigonometric, exponential and hyperbolic functions; graphs of the elementary functions and geometric transformations of the same
Sequences: topology; limits and related theorems; monotonic sequences; Bolzano-Weierstrass and Cauchy theorems; basic examples; the Neper number "e"; recursive sequences; complex sequences

Continuous functions: limits of functions; continuity and properties of continuous functions (including intermediate values, Weierstrass theorem); uniform continuity and Heine-Cantor theorem; Lipschitz continuity; infinitesimals
Properties of differentiable functions (including Rolle, Lagrange, Hopital theorems)
Taylor expansion (with Peano and Lagrange remainder)
Indefinite and definite integral: definition and computation (straightforward, by parts, by change of variables)
Generalised integrals: definition and comparison principles
Numerical series: definition, convergence criteria, Leibniz and integral criteria
assessment_rules: The written exam is passed with a grade of 18 or higher. The oral exam will evaluate understanding of the course content, the use of correct mathematical formalism, and appropriate language. The final grade will be a weighted average of the written and oral exams. The assessment aims to measure achievement of learning outcomes, particularly points 1 to 4.
